extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners seeking MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under Step 2B of the §101 (subject matter eligibility) framework, including when elements are 'well‑understood, routine, conventional', what counts as meaningful limitations, and when claims are merely instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well‑understood, routine, conventional activity. This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, and insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze additional elements to determine if they merely recite activities widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry. If elements are beyond those recognized as well‑understood/routine/conventional, they will generally favor eligibility. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for more on formulating rejections based on this consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known‑in‑the‑art elements can still be unconventional (novelty/obviousness distinct from eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of elements) that is known in the art can nonetheless be unconventional or non‑routine for purposes of eligibility; novelty/obviousness inquiries are separate from eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may improve conventional computer functionality even if anticipated by prior art (e.g., Enfish). Examiners should consider whether features provide technical benefits (faster searches, reduced memory, etc.) that reflect an improvement rather than treating mere prior‑art teaching as dispositive against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual determination required and must be supported in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual finding is required to conclude that an additional element (or combination) is well‑understood, routine, conventional activity, and that finding must be expressly supported in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate support includes: (a) citations to applicant specification or statements during prosecution; (b) citations to court decisions noting the conventional nature; (c) citations to publications demonstrating conventionality; or (d) a statement that the examiner is taking official notice. See MPEP §2106.07(a), and cases such as Berkheimer and related precedent. The examiner may rely on their expertise and need not always perform a prior art search if the conventional nature is readily apparent to one skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of 'widely prevalent' or 'common use' analogous to 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination that an element is well‑understood/routine/conventional uses the same analysis as whether an element is so well known that it need not be described in detail in the specification under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should conclude an element is conventional only when they can readily conclude — based on expertise, specification statements, or authoritative sources — that the element is widely prevalent or commonly used in the relevant industry. Mere discussion in a few journals or limited use by a few scientists is not necessarily sufficient to render a technique routine in the field (example: novel glucose‑sensing earring vs. routine glucose monitoring techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of conventional elements may provide an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are well‑understood, routine, conventional when considered separately, their particular combination may amount to an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider elements both individually and in combination. New combinations of known steps can be patentable (Diamond v. Diehr). Examples: repeating freeze‑thaw cycles contrary to the art (CellzDirect/Rapid Litigation) or non‑conventional arrangement of generic network components providing technical improvement (BASCOM). If the combination yields a non‑generic function or technical improvement, it may favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer functions commonly recognized as well‑understood/routine when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have identified certain computer functions as well‑understood, routine, conventional activities when recited at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: receiving/transmitting data over a network (using Internet to gather data; forwarding information), performing repetitive calculations, electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining accounts or logs), storing and retrieving information in memory, scanning/extracting data from documents (OCR), and standard web‑browser navigation (back/forward). However, not all computer functions are conventional — claims specifying how interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result or providing technical details may be eligible (see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Life‑science laboratory techniques commonly recognized as well‑understood/routine when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, courts have recognized various laboratory techniques as well‑understood, routine, conventional activities when claimed at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: determining biomarker levels in blood by any means, using PCR to amplify/detect DNA, detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample, immunizing a patient, analyzing DNA for sequence/variants, freezing and thawing cells, amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids, and hybridizing a gene probe. When recited generically these techniques may not provide 'significantly more' unless tied to specific, unconventional applications or integration into treatment/prophylaxis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other non‑technical activities recognized as conventional when claimed generically
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found commonplace non‑technical activities to be well‑understood/routine when claimed at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: recording a customer's order, shuffling/dealing a deck of cards, restricting public access by requiring viewing of an ad, presenting offers and gathering statistics, determining estimated outcomes and setting prices, and arranging/sorting information or pricing hierarchies. Generic recitation of these activities often will not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Meaningful Limitations — claim must add meaningful limitations beyond mere linkage to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent‑eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)‑(d) (improvement, integration into practical application, etc.) qualify as meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more. Examples: Diehr (arrhenius equation applied in automated rubber‑molding process — steps that limited application to a practical molding process were meaningful) and Classen (immunization integrated into a specific, tangible method). Examiners should explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the exception and assess both individual elements and their combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that are nothing more than a recitation to 'apply' a judicial exception (e.g., ‘apply it’ on a generic computer) or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer do not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (Alice, Mayo, Benson) emphasize that to be eligible the claim must do more than state the exception and add words that 'apply it.' Examples: Mayo (measuring metabolite levels by any known process was routine and amounted to application without inventive concept), Alice (intermediated settlement implemented on generic computer was merely applying the abstract idea). Note that eligibility does not require claim narrowness — some broad claims have been held eligible when they include meaningful technical improvements (e.g., McRO, Thales Visionix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection standard — only reject when examiner can conclude 'no significantly more' and support the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection under Step 2B should only be made if the examiner, relying on expertise and supported factual findings, can conclude that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making such a rejection, the examiner should provide written support for factual determinations (specification citations, case law, publications, or official notice) and consider overlap with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions, insignificant extra‑solution activity). See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulation guidance.
